stages.notes: Team time trial with individual times. Uphill finish past Montjuïc Castle — the finish climb is uncategorised in a TTT, no KOM points awarded.
Côte de Bègues (Cat2) mid-stage; Montjuïc Castle (Cat3) climbed three times in the circuit finale.
Four categorised climbs. Col de Toses is the main difficulty before the Col du Calvaire crosses the Spain–France border; short uphill summit finish at Les Angles.
Four categorised climbs through the Pyrenean foothills. Col de Montségur is the key difficulty, 36km from the finish in Foix.
Côte de Baleix (1km, 8.8%) with 26km to the line; sprint finish in Pau.
Classic Pyrenean day. Aspin then Tourmalet (Souvenir Jacques Goddet), followed by the new Gavarnie-Gèdre summit finish — a long valley climb whose low average hides the fatigue from the Tourmalet.
Côte de Béguey (Cat4) ~38km from the line; sprint finish into Bordeaux.
Côte de Domme and Côte du Buisson-de-Cadouin (both Cat4) mid-stage; flat run-in to the sprint finish.
Four categorised climbs across the Corrèze plateau. Suc au May (Cat2) is the key test before Rest Day 1.
Bastille Day in the Massif Central. Seven categorised climbs including Puy Mary – Pas de Peyrol (Cat1) and Col de Pertus (Cat1) before the Col de Font de Cère finale into Le Lioran.
Two Cat4 climbs (Billonnière early on, Billy-Chevannes ~38km out); sprint expected in Nevers.
Three Cat4 climbs on the Burgundy plateau (Lanty, Cuzy, Montagny-lès-Buxy); sprint in Chalon. Starts at the former F1 circuit.
Longest stage of the race. Ballon d'Alsace — the Tour's very first mountain (1904) — crests ~30km from the finish in Belfort. First of two ascents in 2026.

Four Vosges climbs: Grand Ballon (highest point in the range), Col du Page (new to the Tour), Ballon d'Alsace (second ascent in 2026), and Col du Haag (new to the Tour). Finish descends 5.9km from Col du Haag to Le Markstein.

New HC summit finish on the Plateau de Solaison Brison — the steepest average gradient of any 2026 summit finish. Le Salève – Col de la Croisette (11.2%) is the steepest categorised climb on the entire route.
Individual Time Trial along Lake Geneva. Côte de Larringes (Cat2) is the sole categorised climb and also acts as an intermediate time check.
Four short climbs through the Savoie and Chartreuse (Bassa, Rossillon, Col des Prés, Saint-Jean-d'Arvey) before the descent into Voiron to open the final Alpine block.
Opens the final Alpine block. Côte d'Engins (Cat1) and three further climbs build to the steady summit finish at Orcières-Merlette (~10 hairpins, even gradient).
Col Bayard (Cat2), Col du Noyer (Cat1), Col d'Ornon (Cat2), then the full 21-hairpin ascent of Alpe d'Huez.

Queen stage. Croix de Fer – Télégraphe – Galibier (Souvenir Henri Desgrange; highest point of the 2026 Tour at 2642m) – Sarenne, then the non-categorised final approach to Alpe d'Huez via the Sarenne road.
Côte du Pavé des Gardes early on; Butte Montmartre climbed three times in the circuit finale before the Champs-Élysées finish.
Grande Partenza in Bulgaria — the first time in race history. First maglia rosa decided in a bunch sprint.
Second longest stage of the race. Lyaskovets Monastery climb inside the final 10km — steep opening section with double-digit gradients near the bottom.
The sole climb is the long, steady Borovets Pass. Sprint finish in the Bulgarian capital.
First stage on Italian soil after the Bulgarian transfer. Cozzo Tunno (14km, 5.9%) climbed mid-stage.
Montagna Grande di Viggiano is the key climb, 50km from the line — nearly 7km with sections above 10%.
Early Cava de' Tirreni climb (Cat 4) but a sprint finish on the Naples seafront.
Longest Grand Tour stage since 2021. First true GC day — Roccaraso (Cat 2) mid-stage then summit finish on the Blockhaus via Roccamorice. Final 10km consistently near or above 10%.
Final 60km packed with Muri-style climbs: Montefiore dell'Aso, Monterubbiano, Capodarco, then the punchy Fermo finish (max 22%).
Summit finish in the Apennines. Final 3km of Corno alle Scale are in double-digit gradients.
Sole ITT of the race — flat, coastal, and quick. Wind can be a significant factor on this exposed seafront course.
Classic breakaway stage through Liguria. Passo del Termine, Colle di Guaitarola (Cat 2) and Colla dei Scioli before the Chiavari finish.
Colle Giovo and Bric Berton (both Cat 3) but a fast enough finale to keep the sprinters in play.
Bieno and Ungiasca inside the last 25km; flat run-in to the lake at Verbania.

Five-star mountain stage. Climbing starts almost from the gun up the Col du Saint-Barthélemy (Cat 1, 15.8km), then Doues, Lin Noir (Cat 1), Verrogne, and the Pila summit finish — first Giro summit finish at Pila in approximately 30 years.
Flattest stage of the race. Finishes with laps in Milan.
Entirely in Switzerland (Canton Ticino). Torre and Leontica climbed twice on a circuit before the Cari summit finish.
Passo dei Tre Termini and Cocca di Lodrino mid-stage, then long transitional terrain through Trentino to the Andalo-Lever summit finish.
Fastro (Le Scale di Primolano) mid-stage, then the Prosecco hills. The Muro di Ca' del Poggio — short, brutal, and beloved — comes inside the final 10km.
Queen stage. Passo Duran – Coi – Forcella Staulanza – Passo Giau (Cima Coppi, 2236m) – Passo Falzarego – Piani di Pezzè summit finish. Five consecutive climbs in the final 100km.
Penultimate mountain stage. Piancavallo is climbed twice — the second ascent is the final GC verdict before Rome.
Ceremonial finale on a circuit in Rome. The Maglia Rosa is celebrated on the streets of the Eternal City.
Opening time trial through the Principality's streets — technical, with the first race leader decided by seconds.
Longest stage of the race. Technical start through Nice before Provence's rolling lavender country; two Cat3 climbs (Alto Châteauneuf-Grasse, Col de Saint Andrieu) should suit the fast finishers.
Flat start gradually rising into the Pyrénées Orientales. Col de Mont-Louis (Cat1) sets up the first summit finish of the race at Font Romeu (Cat2), 1,937m.

Short but brutal loop entirely within Andorra: Port d'Envalira (Cat1, the highest paved pass in the Pyrenees), Collada de Beixalís (Cat1) and Coll d'Ordino (Cat1) before a short finishing ramp at Alto de La Comella (Cat3).
Alto de Paüls (Cat3) is the only real difficulty; likely a sprint finish in the Terres de l'Ebre.
Puerto de la Serratella and Alto del Desierto de las Palmas (both Cat2) before a dirt-road finale up Puerto El Bartolo (Cat1, 3km unpaved) and a fast descent into Castelló.
Second summit finish of the race, climbing into Teruel's Sierra de Gúdar via Puerto El Remolcador and Puerto de San Rafael (both Cat2) before the ski-station finish at Valdelinares.
Last chance for the sprinters in week one; Puerto de Barx (Cat2) crests just before the finish in Xeraco.

Brutal way to close the first week — six categorised climbs and nearly 5,000m of climbing, including Puerto de El Miserat (Cat1), before the legendary Alto de Aitana summit finish above the Costa Blanca.
Winding stage through Albacete province after the first rest day; three Cat3 climbs (Puerto del Peralejo, Puerto de Aýna, Puerto de Socovos) could suit a breakaway.
Another sprint opportunity, but Alto del Morrón de Totana (Cat3) crests just 30km from the finish.
Andalucía's toughest welcome: the traditional Velefique–Calar Alto double, climbing to Europe's largest astronomical observatory at over 2,100m.
Winding stage that front-loads its difficulty — Venta de la Cebada (Cat1) and Alto del Legionario (Cat2) come in the first half, with a flatter run to Loja.
One of La Vuelta's most decisive summit finishes since 2002 — Puerto de Los Villares and Puerto de Locubín (both Cat2) set up the final ramps to Sierra de la Pandera.
Sierra Morena classic-style stage with three Cat3 climbs before the traditional reduced-group finish in Córdoba, on the eve of the second rest day.

stages.finish: La Rábida. Palos de la Frontera
stages.notes: One of the last chances for the sprinters — winding through Huelva's hills before a flat run along the coast to the Columbus monuments at La Rábida.
The flattest stage of the race; an early breakaway is the main variable before a bunch sprint through Seville's streets.
Second and final time trial, along the Cádiz coastline where the wind could make real time differences among the GC contenders.
Flat and coastal for most of the day before the Serranía de Ronda piles on the fatigue ahead of the final climb to Peñas Blancas (Cat1) — scene of Richard Carapaz's 2022 stage win.

Route revised after a landslide closed the road to Alto de Hazallanas — the stage now climbs Puerto de Los Blancares, Puerto de El Purche twice, and the new Puerto de El Duque, before the same unprecedented summit finish at Collado del Alguacil — 8.3km at 9.8%.
Ceremonial-style final stage with a circuit finish past the Alhambra, crowning the winner of La Vuelta 26 in Granada.

climbs.name: Côte du Stade Olympique de Montjuïc
climbs.notes: TTT finish climb — officially uncategorised (no KOM points are awarded in a team time trial). Short ramp to the Olympic stadium.

climbs.name: Côte du Château de Montjuïc
climbs.notes: Climbed three times in the finale — first at km 141.6, then km 153.8, then km 166 at the finish.

climbs.name: Côte de Sant Feliu de Codines
climbs.notes: Early stage climb before the Pyrenees proper.

climbs.name: Col de Toses (Collada de Toses)
climbs.notes: Main difficulty of Stage 3.

climbs.name: Col du Calvaire
climbs.notes: Crosses the Spain–France border on the approach to Les Angles.

climbs.name: Les Angles
climbs.notes: Short summit finish.

climbs.name: Col de Montségur
climbs.notes: Key difficulty of the day, 36km from Foix.

climbs.name: Côte de Baleix
climbs.notes: Short, punchy climb 26km from the sprint finish in Pau.

climbs.name: Col d'Aspin
climbs.notes: Climbed from the Arreau side.

climbs.name: Col du Tourmalet
climbs.notes: Via Sainte-Marie-de-Campan / La Mongie. Souvenir Jacques Goddet at the summit. Final 10km averages near 9%.

climbs.name: Gavarnie-Gèdre
climbs.notes: New summit finish for 2026. Long valley climb — low average gradient hides the fatigue accumulated from the Tourmalet.

climbs.name: Côte de Béguey
climbs.notes: Sole categorised climb on the sprint stage to Bordeaux.

climbs.name: Suc au May
climbs.notes: Key climb of the day.

climbs.name: Côte de la Croix du Pey
Mont Bessou
climbs.notes: Summit of the Millevaches plateau — very gentle ramp.

climbs.name: Puy Mary – Pas de Peyrol
climbs.notes: Via D680-D17. Final 2km ramp near 9%.

climbs.name: Col de Pertus
climbs.notes: Steepest climb of the day.

climbs.name: Col de Font de Cère
climbs.notes: Leads directly into the Le Lioran finish.

climbs.name: Ballon d'Alsace
climbs.notes: First of two ascents in 2026 (also Stage 14). The Tour's very first mountain, used in the 1904 edition.

climbs.name: Grand Ballon
climbs.notes: Highest point in the Vosges. Uneven profile — last 6km near 8%.

climbs.name: Col du Page
climbs.notes: New to the Tour in 2026.

climbs.name: Ballon d'Alsace
climbs.notes: Second ascent in 2026 (also Stage 13). The Tour's very first mountain, 1904.

climbs.name: Col du Haag
climbs.notes: New to the Tour in 2026. Via VC-D431. Uneven gradient with sections to 15%.

climbs.name: Le Salève – Col de la Croisette
climbs.notes: Steepest categorised climb on the entire 2026 route.

climbs.name: Plateau de Solaison Brison
climbs.notes: New HC summit finish — steepest summit-finish average of the 2026 race. Max gradient ~12%. One of two HC summit finishes.

climbs.name: Côte de Larringes
climbs.notes: Sole categorised climb of the ITT; also acts as intermediate time check point 2.

climbs.name: Côte d'Engins
climbs.notes: First categorised climb of the day; long and steady.

climbs.name: Orcières-Merlette
climbs.notes: Steady, even gradient with approximately 10 hairpins.

climbs.name: Col Bayard
climbs.notes: First climb of the day from Gap.

climbs.name: Col du Noyer
climbs.notes: Sharpest regular pass of the 2026 race.

climbs.name: Alpe d'Huez
climbs.notes: Classic 21-hairpin ascent via Le Bourg-d'Oisans. First 2km near 10%; hairpins 10–11 hit double digits.

climbs.name: Col de la Croix de Fer
climbs.notes: Long and irregular — the length matters more than the gradient.

climbs.name: Col du Télégraphe
climbs.notes: Runs almost straight into the Galibier.

climbs.name: Col du Galibier
climbs.notes: Highest point of the 2026 Tour at 2642m. Souvenir Henri Desgrange awarded at the summit.

climbs.name: Col de Sarenne
climbs.notes: Previously only used as a descent (2013) — first time climbed in competition. Leads into the non-categorised final approach to Alpe d'Huez.

climbs.name: Côte de la Butte Montmartre
climbs.notes: Climbed three times in the finale — at km 90.8, km 106.7, and km 122.7 at the finish.

climbs.name: Cape Agalina (1st)
climbs.notes: First categorised climb of the 2026 Giro on the Black Sea coast. Max gradient 10%.

climbs.name: Cape Agalina (2nd)
climbs.notes: Second passage of the same coastal climb. Max gradient 11%.

climbs.name: Byala Pass
climbs.notes: First significant climb of the stage. Steady ascent through the Rose Valley. Max gradient 14%.

climbs.name: Vratnik Pass
climbs.notes: Longest climb of the Bulgarian stages. Max gradient 11%.

climbs.name: Lyaskovets Monastery Pass
climbs.notes: Double-digit gradient near the bottom of this steep final climb before the descent to Veliko Tarnovo. Max gradient 11%.

climbs.name: Borovets Pass
climbs.notes: Long and steady — the only climb of Stage 3, leading into the Borovets ski area. Max gradient 9%.

climbs.name: Cozzo Tunno
climbs.notes: A long steady drag rather than steep. Max gradient 15%. Climbed mid-stage.

climbs.name: Prestieri
climbs.notes: Opening categorised climb of Stage 5 — long and manageable, entering the Parco del Pollino. Max gradient 8%.

climbs.name: Montagna Grande di Viggiano
climbs.notes: Key climb of the stage, about 50km from the line. Nearly 7km with stretches above 10%. Max gradient 12%.

climbs.name: Cava de' Tirreni
climbs.notes: Early-stage climb through the hills above Cava de' Tirreni. Max gradient 8%.

climbs.name: Roccaraso
climbs.notes: Long valley climb through Abruzzo before the final approach to Blockhaus. Max gradient 12%.

climbs.name: Blockhaus (via Roccamorice)
climbs.notes: One of the Giro's great summit finishes. Final 10km consistently near or above 10%. Max gradient 14%.

climbs.name: Montefiore dell'Aso
climbs.notes: Long drag through the Marche hills. Max gradient 12%.

climbs.name: Monterubbiano
climbs.notes: Muri-style climb through a medieval hilltop village. Max gradient 12%.

climbs.name: Capodarco
climbs.notes: Short and punchy in the final run-in to Fermo. Max gradient 18%.

climbs.name: Fermo
climbs.notes: Irregular finish climb to the medieval hill town on narrow porphyry streets. Max gradient 22%.

climbs.name: Querciola
climbs.notes: Long penultimate climb before Corno alle Scale. Max gradient 15%.

climbs.name: Corno alle Scale
climbs.notes: Irregular profile — final 3km ramp into double-digit gradients. Max gradient 15%.

climbs.name: Passo del Termine
climbs.notes: Crosses the Cinque Terre ridge. Max gradient 10%.

climbs.name: Colle di Guaitarola
climbs.notes: Second climb through the Cinque Terre area — longest of the stage. Max gradient 11%.

climbs.name: Colla dei Scioli
climbs.notes: Short and steep approach to the Chiavari finish. Max gradient 15%.

climbs.name: Colle Giovo
climbs.notes: First significant climb of Stage 12, exiting the Ligurian coast near Savona. Max gradient 10%.

climbs.name: Bric Berton
climbs.notes: Drops the peloton from the Ligurian ridge into the Po plain towards Novi Ligure. Max gradient 10%.

climbs.name: Bieno
climbs.notes: Short but sharp — inside the last 25km. Max gradient 13%.

climbs.name: Ungiasca
climbs.notes: Backroads with sections often above 10% near the top. Max gradient 13%.

climbs.name: Col du Saint-Barthélemy
climbs.notes: Climbing begins almost from the gun — the stage starts ascending within the first 2km. 1029m of elevation gain. Max gradient 12%.

climbs.name: Doues
climbs.notes: Least demanding climb of the day after the Saint-Barthélemy descent. Max gradient 12%.

climbs.name: Lin Noir
climbs.notes: No real descent before the next climb — riders hit Verrogne immediately after. Max gradient 12%.

climbs.name: Verrogne
climbs.notes: Connects Lin Noir to the Pila summit finish. Max gradient 11%.

climbs.name: Pila (Gressan side)
climbs.notes: First Giro summit finish at Pila in approximately 30 years. Final 3km average 9–11%. Max gradient 10%.

climbs.name: Torre (1st ascent)
climbs.notes: First of two passages on the circuit. Max gradient 10%.

climbs.name: Leontica (1st ascent)
climbs.notes: First of two passages — steeper than Torre. Max gradient 14%.

climbs.name: Torre (2nd ascent)
climbs.notes: Second passage on the same road. Max gradient 10%.

climbs.name: Leontica (2nd ascent)
climbs.notes: Second passage before the final push to Carì. Max gradient 14%.

climbs.name: Carì
climbs.notes: Summit finish after the Torre/Leontica circuit. Max gradient 13%.

climbs.name: Passo dei Tre Termini
climbs.notes: First climb of Stage 17, after the flat run-in past Lake Iseo. Max gradient 9%.

climbs.name: Cocca di Lodrino
climbs.notes: Second climb before entering the Chiese river valley. Max gradient 9%.

climbs.name: Andalo-Lever
climbs.notes: Final categorised climb, leading into the Andalo plateau. Max gradient 9%.

climbs.name: Fastro (Le Scale di Primolano)
climbs.notes: Short climb through the Valstagna gorge area. Max gradient 9%.

climbs.name: Muro di Ca' del Poggio
climbs.notes: Short and brutal. A staple Prosecco hills finale climb. Max gradient 19%.

climbs.name: Passo Duran
climbs.notes: Long stretches nudging double digits throughout. Max gradient 14%.

climbs.name: Coi
climbs.notes: Steep and demanding. Max gradient 19%.

climbs.name: Forcella Staulanza
climbs.notes: Links the Coi descent to the Passo Giau. Max gradient 10%.

climbs.name: Passo Giau
climbs.notes: Cima Coppi — highest point of the 2026 Giro at 2236m. Last used in 2021. Outstanding views over the Dolomites. Max gradient 14%.

climbs.name: Passo Falzarego
climbs.notes: Relatively straightforward after the Giau descent. Max gradient 10%.

climbs.name: Piani di Pezzè
climbs.notes: Summit finish. Final kilometre averages near 11%. Max gradient 12.2%.

climbs.name: Clauzetto
climbs.notes: Early-stage climb through the Friulian hills. Max gradient 9%.

climbs.name: Piancavallo (1st ascent)
climbs.notes: Climbed with approximately 53km remaining. Max gradient 14%.

climbs.name: Piancavallo (2nd ascent)
climbs.notes: Same profile as the first ascent — decides the final GC of the race. Max gradient 14%.

climbs.name: Alto Châteauneuf-Grasse
climbs.notes: Gradual foothill climb above the Riviera.

climbs.name: Col de Saint Andrieu
climbs.notes: Length/gradient from Komoot's GPS route data (confirmed by Robin as climb #6 on the official Komoot stage map).

climbs.name: Col de Mont-Louis
climbs.notes: Steady mid-mountain grind via Fontpédrouse; sets up the descent into Font Romeu.

climbs.name: Font Romeu
climbs.notes: First summit finish of the race. Short final rise off the Mont-Louis descent — matches organisers' own description of the last km easing to around 4.5%. Length/gradient from Komoot's GPS route data (best-guess match by position — not independently cross-checked against another source).

climbs.name: Port d'Envalira
climbs.notes: The highest paved pass in the Pyrenees. Long and steady from Andorra la Vella via El Tarter — altitude is the real difficulty, not the gradient.

climbs.name: Collada de Beixalís
climbs.notes: Irregular, narrow road via Encamp with hairpins and ramps over 20% — the toughest climb of the day pound for pound.

climbs.name: Coll d'Ordino
climbs.notes: Steady lower slopes via Ordino, harder in the closing kilometres. Steepest section 10.7%.

climbs.name: Alto de La Comella
climbs.notes: Short finishing ramp back into Andorra la Vella. Length/gradient from Komoot's route elevation data (unofficial, not yet cross-checked against another source).

climbs.name: Alto de Paüls
climbs.notes: Length/gradient from Komoot.

climbs.name: Puerto de la Serratella
climbs.notes: Long, gradual ascent — categorised more for cumulative altitude gain than steepness.

climbs.name: Coll de la Bandereta
climbs.notes: Climbed from the west (Rosildos side) before descending to Benlloch, confirmed against the route map. Max gradient 9.6%.

climbs.name: Alto del Desierto de las Palmas
climbs.notes: Climbed from Benicàssim on the coast.

climbs.name: Puerto El Bartolo
climbs.notes: First-ever dirt-road finale for La Vuelta — the final ~3.5km run on gravel/sterrato before a fast paved descent into Castelló. Steepest ramp 17.2%.

climbs.name: Alto de Zucaina
climbs.notes: Length/gradient from Komoot.

climbs.name: Puerto Fuente de Rubielos
climbs.notes: Gradual, sustained ascent.

climbs.name: Puerto de San Rafael
climbs.notes: Long false-flat approach before the road continues on to the Valdelinares finish.

climbs.name: Aramón Valdelinares
climbs.notes: Summit finish at the Sierra de Gúdar ski station, climbed via Puerto de San Rafael from Mora de Rubielos. Length/gradient from Komoot's GPS route data — the last (and only major) climb on this stage, so a confident match for the actual finish ascent, replacing an earlier figure that was mistakenly for the Alcalá de la Selva side.

climbs.name: Puerto de Barx
climbs.notes: Crests just before the finish in Xeraco. Length/gradient from Komoot.

climbs.name: Puerto de Tárbena
climbs.notes: Gradual, early climb of the day.

climbs.name: Puerto de El Miserat
climbs.notes: Long and gradual rather than steep — the Cat1 reflects length and cumulative altitude gain.

climbs.name: Puerto de Tollos
climbs.notes: Climbed from the north — length/gradient from Komoot, cross-checked against CyclingCols' matching "North, from CV-712/CV-713" profile (4.8km/4.5%).

climbs.name: Puerto de Tudons
climbs.notes: Length/gradient from Komoot, the specific final segment up to the summit (not the much longer climb-from-the-stage-start figure CyclingCols lists).

climbs.name: Puerto de Benifallim
climbs.notes: Gradual approach into the closing kilometres before Aitana.

climbs.name: Alto de Aitana
climbs.notes: One of Spain's hardest summit finishes, used by La Vuelta in 2015, 2019 and 2021. Long, irregular grind with a max gradient around 9.2%.

climbs.name: Puerto del Peralejo
climbs.notes: Very gradual climb from Fábricas de Riópar — length/gradient from CyclingCols, confirmed as the correct approach side by matching the stage's actual direction of travel. Max gradient 9.2%.

climbs.name: Puerto de Socovos
climbs.notes: Length/gradient from Komoot, the final segment leading to the summit. A separate, earlier rise (1.74km at 6%) also appears before it on the same approach.

climbs.name: Alto del Morrón de Totana
climbs.notes: Crests around 30km from the finish in Lorca.

climbs.name: Alto del Cabecico
climbs.notes: Length/gradient from Komoot.

climbs.name: Alto Cóbdar
climbs.notes: Length/gradient from Komoot.

climbs.name: Collado García
climbs.notes: Length/gradient from Komoot, combining two consecutive detected segments (1.53km + 2.62km, both ~5%) into one continuous climb.

climbs.name: Alto de Velefique
climbs.notes: Climbed from Velefique town, cresting before a descent toward Bacares and the final push to Calar Alto. Length/gradient from CyclingCols' "South, from Velefique" profile — an exact match for this stage's approach town. Max gradient 11.0%.

climbs.name: Calar Alto
climbs.notes: Summit finish at Europe's largest astronomical observatory, over 2,100m — one of the hardest climbs in the south of Spain. Length/gradient calculated from Komoot's elevation chart between the Bacares altitude/distance markers (1,196m to the 2,134m summit) — a strong match to the roadbook's own Bacares altitude of 1,197m.

climbs.name: Alto del Legionario
climbs.notes: Long, gradual ascent via Padul.

climbs.name: Puerto de Locubín
climbs.notes: Leads into the final push to Sierra de la Pandera.

climbs.name: Sierra de la Pandera
climbs.notes: One of La Vuelta's classic brutal summit finishes since 2002, with several sectors over 15% — including inside the final kilometre, where it touches 18%.

climbs.name: Puerto de la Forestal
climbs.notes: Gradual climb into the Sierra Morena.

climbs.name: Alto de Villaviciosa de Córdoba
climbs.notes: Length/gradient calculated from Komoot's elevation chart between the base and summit markers.

climbs.name: Puerto Artafi
climbs.notes: Length/gradient calculated from Komoot's elevation chart for the correct (stage-direction) side — a different, steeper segment than CyclingCols' only listed profile, which climbs the opposite way from Medina Azahara.

climbs.name: Sierra de Aracena climb 1
climbs.notes: Komoot-detected climb segment (Climbs & Descents panel) — genuinely uncategorised by the race, not large enough to be awarded an official category.

climbs.name: Sierra de Aracena climb 7
climbs.notes: Last of the seven detected climbs — after this the route flattens out for the coastal run to La Rábida.

climbs.name: Puerto del Viento
climbs.notes: Climbed from the east, from El Burgo. Length/gradient from CyclingCols. Max gradient 9.6%.

climbs.name: Peñas Blancas
climbs.notes: Scene of Richard Carapaz's stage win in 2022, extended a few km longer than the 2013 version. Starts almost at sea level in Estepona; several ramps over 14%.

climbs.name: Puerto de Los Blancares
climbs.notes: Unaffected by the stage-20 landslide reroute. Length/gradient from Komoot's elevation chart for the correct (Guadix-side) direction.

climbs.name: Puerto de El Purche (1st ascent)
climbs.notes: Climbed via Huétor Vega. Length/gradient from Komoot's GPS route data.

climbs.name: Puerto de El Purche (2nd ascent)
climbs.notes: Second ascent of the day, same climb as earlier.

climbs.name: Puerto de El Duque
climbs.notes: Never before climbed in Vuelta history. Ascends the same Genil River valley as Alto de Hazallanas, with an identical final 2km finishing on the same road to the Sierra Nevada ski resort — but shorter and slightly easier, and without the 18-19% ramps that mark Hazallanas' opening kilometres after the technical descent from Güéjar Sierra.

climbs.name: Collado del Alguacil
climbs.notes: Unprecedented summit finish and La Vuelta 26's last great challenge — 8.3km at an official average of 9.8%.
